scenes.text: In 1993, a game called Doom ran on a computer with four megabytes of memory.
That's about the size of a single photo on your phone.
There was no 3D accelerator. The main processor did all the rendering.
Today, a developer starts with an engine, like Unity or Unreal, that takes care of graphics, sound, memory and the hardware.
On DOS, all of that was the developer's problem. And quite often, the player's too.
So how hard was it to make a game for DOS?
Let's start with memory, because memory was a mess.
The original IBM PC, from 1981, could address one megabyte of memory.
But only the first six hundred and forty kilobytes were meant for programs.
The other three hundred and eighty-four were reserved for video memory, expansion cards and the BIOS.
For more than a decade, DOS normally started programs inside that space. Anything beyond it took extra work.
That's where the famous line comes from. 640K ought to be enough for anybody.
It's usually credited to Bill Gates. There's no record that he ever said it, and he denies it.
By the early nineties, a PC came with four megabytes, or eight.
And a game could still stop with the words "not enough memory".
Having the memory and being able to use it were two different things.
One way around it was expanded memory, or EMS.
A sixty-four kilobyte window sat in the upper part of that first megabyte. Through it, a program could see four pages of extra memory, sixteen kilobytes each,
and swap them for others, like turning the pages of a book through a hole in a sheet of paper.
Another way was extended memory, reached through a driver called HIMEM.
And this is where the developer's problem became the player's.
Drivers for the mouse, the CD drive or the sound card took a bite out of that precious memory, unless you managed to load them high.
So players learned to edit two files, CONFIG.SYS and AUTOEXEC.BAT.
One game wanted EMS. Another wanted it switched off, with a setting called NOEMS. And a third needed every free kilobyte.
In 1993, MS-DOS 6 added a menu at startup.
You picked the configuration for the game you wanted to play, and the computer started up for that game.
Some people ended up with a separate entry for almost every game they owned.
But by then, the bigger games had found a way around the limits of DOS.
Since the 386, the processor itself could run in 32-bit protected mode, with room for up to four gigabytes.
We've looked at protected mode in an earlier video. DOS, though, couldn't use it.
So games brought their own helper, a DOS extender. The best known was DOS/4GW.
It came bundled with a popular compiler, Watcom C.
When a game started, DOS/4GW switched the processor into protected mode, giving the game access to memory beyond the DOS limit.
DOS was still there underneath, providing services like file access. But the game now ran in protected mode, not as a traditional DOS program.
If you played DOS games in the nineties, you've seen its name flash by on the screen.
Now, the picture. In one of the most widely used VGA modes, called Mode 13h, the screen was three hundred and twenty by two hundred pixels, in two hundred and fifty-six colours.
Each pixel was one byte. To colour a pixel, you wrote a number into memory. No graphics library. Just memory.
The whole screen took sixty-four thousand bytes.
That's just under sixty-four kilobytes, small enough to fit in one segment, the block a 16-bit program could address in one go. For once, memory was on your side.
But if you draw straight onto the visible screen, the player sees half-finished pictures, and the image flickers.
So games drew each frame in a hidden buffer first, then copied the finished image into video memory.
In 1991, Michael Abrash, a programmer and writer, published a better way. He called it Mode X.
It used a part of the VGA that most programmers had never touched.
It gave square pixels, and room for several screens in video memory.
The game drew on a screen nobody could see, and then simply switched to it. But it was much harder to program.
Then there was sound. And sound was a lottery.
The PC's own speaker was built to beep.
Then came sound cards, and other sound hardware. No two of them worked the same way.
AdLib, with a Yamaha chip that synthesised music. Sound Blaster, which could also play recorded sound.
The Roland MT-32, an expensive box with richer instruments. The Gravis UltraSound.
Supporting all of them meant writing different drivers.
And the game had to know where the card was. Its port, its interrupt, and its DMA channel.
The usual answer, for a Sound Blaster, was port 220, IRQ 7, DMA 1. Usually.
Get one of them wrong, and the game was silent. Or it froze.
In 1991, a programmer called John Miles released a library that talked to many sound cards through a single interface.
A game could write its sound code once, and let the library deal with the card.
It was another layer between the game and the hardware. Keep that in mind.
And then there was speed. Programmers counted every step the processor took.
To find a pixel on the screen, you multiply its row by three hundred and twenty.
On older processors, multiplying could be expensive.
But three hundred and twenty is two hundred and fifty-six plus sixty-four. Both are powers of two.
So you can replace the multiplication with two bit shifts and an addition.
Chris Sawyer went all the way down to the metal. He wrote Transport Tycoon, in 1994, almost entirely in assembly language,
the instructions the processor itself understands, one by one.
And sometimes, even all of that wasn't enough.
In 1990, Wing Commander had a bug that the team couldn't find, with the deadline close.
When you quit the game, the memory manager crashed with an error message.
So a programmer, Ken Demarest, opened the memory manager in a hex editor and changed the text of that message.
Now it said: "Thank you for playing Wing Commander."
Then the team found the real bug, and the joke never shipped.
Some players are still sure they saw it. And later Origin games really did say goodbye like that.
Which brings us back to Doom.
Doom used DOS/4GW, and ran as a 32-bit program.
Floating-point hardware wasn't guaranteed on every PC.
So Doom used fixed-point arithmetic. Whole numbers, with the lower sixteen bits standing for the fraction.
And its world wasn't really three-dimensional.
Every level is a flat floor plan, with a height for each floor and each ceiling.
One room can never sit above another. And you can't properly look up or down.
Before a level could be played, a tool cut the map into a binary tree, a BSP.
The engine walks that tree from front to back, starting on the player's side, and skips areas that can't be seen.
And Doom wasn't even written on DOS.
id Software built it on NeXT workstations, and compiled the result for DOS.
Doom wasn't a general 3D engine. It was built for exactly one kind of world. That specialisation helped it run on a 386.
And other studios wanted that world.
Raven Software licensed Doom's engine for Heretic, in 1994, and Hexen, in 1995.
Doom helped establish a new way of making games. Studios could license an existing engine, instead of building it all from scratch.
A memory extender. A sound library. A licensed engine.
Each one took a problem off the developer's hands. And the layers kept growing, into the engines that developers start with today.
So was making games harder back then? In many ways, yes.
But the difficulty didn't disappear. It moved.
Today, developers fight with gigabytes of assets and millions of polygons, instead of a few hundred kilobytes.
On DOS, even the player had to know where their memory went.
So here's a question for you. Do you remember building a boot menu just to get one game running? And was it a struggle, or half the fun? Let me know in the comments.
